summary: Service providers are sometimes legally required to map a subscriber's inside address to the public address they used, but logging every dynamic translation in a Carrier-Grade NAT is heavy. This document describes assigning ports in a predictable, deterministic way so the mapping can be worked out without logging each translation.

eli5.summary: Many homes share a few public addresses. Instead of writing down every time someone borrows one, the provider hands out turns by a fixed rule, so later it can just work out who had which one.

subtitle: Reducing logging overhead in shared IPv4 address systems

tldr.problem: When Carrier-Grade NAT devices share one public IPv4 address among hundreds of customers, logging every connection translation creates massive amounts of data—a 1-million-subscriber provider generates 1.8 petabytes of logs per year—making it hard for operators to respond to abuse reports.
tldr.mechanism: Assign port ranges to subscribers deterministically using a mathematical algorithm, so the mapping can be calculated without logging each connection. Only log exceptions when subscribers exceed their allocated port range.
tldr.outcome: Reduces logging from petabytes to manageable volumes while preserving the ability to identify subscribers for abuse response and public safety investigations.

facts.label: Average connections per customer per day

today: RFC 7422 is an Informational RFC published in December 2014. It describes a practical technique for managing CGN deployments, though IPv6 remains the long-term solution. The RFC has not been obsoleted and is still used in production networks.

sections.title: The Logging Problem in Carrier-Grade NAT
sections.content:
IPv4 address space is nearly exhausted. Many service providers now use Carrier-Grade NAT (CGN) devices that let hundreds of customers share a single public IP address. When a customer makes a connection, the CGN translates their private address to the public address with a different port number.

Providers have a legal duty to respond to abuse complaints: when they receive a report about traffic from a public IP and port, they must trace it back to the customer who sent it. This requires logging every translation. However, the volume is staggering. Research shows customers make about 33,000 connections per day, each log entry is 150-175 bytes, and a million-customer provider generates about 1.8 petabytes of logs annually. This overwhelms storage, network, and search capabilities.
sections.eli5: Many people share one address. The provider must track who used it when to catch bad actors. Writing it all down takes huge space and time.

sections.title: The Deterministic Mapping Approach
sections.content:
Instead of logging every connection, deterministic CGN assigns port ranges to subscribers using a predictable algorithm. The provider configures parameters like the compression ratio (how many customers per public address) and the algorithm type, then calculates which port range belongs to which subscriber.

How it works: When a customer sends a connection, the CGN checks if the port falls in that customer's pre-allocated range. If it does, no log is created—the provider can later reverse the algorithm to figure out the mapping. Only when a customer exceeds their pre-allocated ports and borrows from a shared dynamic pool does the CGN log the translation.

A practical example: if 16 customers share one public address 192.0.2.1 and system ports 0-1023 are reserved, each customer gets about 4,000 ports assigned sequentially. Customer 1 maps to ports 1024-5055, customer 2 to 5056-9087, and so on. To identify customer 1 later, the provider reverses the calculation—no log lookup needed.
sections.eli5: The provider gives each house a range of turns (port numbers). When a house uses its own range, nothing is written down. The provider can always work out which house used which turn by doing the math backwards.

sections.title: Algorithms and Configuration
sections.content:
The RFC defines several algorithms for assigning port ranges, letting operators choose one that fits their needs.

Sequential allocation: The first subscriber gets ports 1024-5055, the second gets 5056-9087, and so on. Simple and fast to reverse, but sequential ports make it easier to guess other customers' ranges.

Staggered allocation: Subscribers receive ports spread across the available range in a pattern, providing better privacy without requiring complex lookups.

Round-robin: A subscriber receives the same port number across multiple public IP addresses in the provider's pool, so a customer using port 2000 might use it across 10 different public addresses.

Other methods: The RFC also describes interlaced (every nth port) and cryptographic random allocation. Each method trades off simplicity for privacy and efficiency.

Operators also configure a dynamic pool factor—extra ports available for customers who use more than their pre-allocated range, such as peer-to-peer users. Only dynamic assignments are logged.
sections.eli5: The provider picks a rule for handing out turns. Sequential is simple but obvious. Other rules mix things up so it is harder to guess. Power users can get extra turns if needed, but those get written down.

sections.title: Operating Deterministic CGN
sections.content:
Operators must log configuration changes. Whenever the inside address range, outside address range, compression ratio, maximum ports, or reserved port list changes, the CGN must create a record with a timestamp. The provider should log the configuration once per day as well, so public safety agencies can find the right configuration when investigating old abuse reports.

Failover is straightforward: because the algorithm is deterministic, a backup CGN can reverse the mapping without additional logs, as long as inside address ranges are unique across failover domains.

Operators should set alarms on port utilization thresholds so they can adjust the algorithm parameters as networks grow. The approach also affects geolocation services: providers using this method must work with geolocation databases to keep mappings up to date when addresses change.

The RFC stresses that while deterministic CGN reduces logging, it is not a replacement for IPv6. Native IPv6 provides subscribers a better experience and eliminates the need for address sharing altogether.
sections.eli5: When the provider changes the rules, that gets written down. Failover is easy because the math still works. The provider watches to make sure the system does not run out of turns, and tells location services when addresses change.
